arXiv:2611.09553v1 [stat.ME] 06 Nov 2026

Risk-set reconstruction balance: zero-targeted diagnostics for artificial censoring in clone–censor–weight analyses

Yuta Nonomiya1,2

1Graduate School of Informatics, Osaka Metropolitan University

2German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence GmbH (DFKI)

Correspondence: Yuta Nonomiya, e-mail: nonomiya.yuta@omu.ac.jp

Abstract. In clone–censor–weight (CCW) analyses, inverse probability of censoring weighting corrects selection from artificial censoring at protocol deviation. Balance diagnostics, such as the end-of-grace between-strategy standardised mean difference (SMD) and censoring balance, compare different populations, and their zero targets under a correct model are not formally stated. We show that, under positivity and a correct censoring model, the weighted retained individuals reconstruct the risk set before each censoring interval and the baseline population, and we propose risk-set reconstruction balance (RRB), which measures how far they depart from these two populations. Interval RRB has a zero target for every history function, including post-baseline covariates, for which between-strategy SMDs have none. Cumulative RRB keeps a zero target for baseline covariates after outcome events, whereas the end-of-grace SMD acquires a depletion term. In simulations, interval RRB responded to an omitted term’s effect on censoring whether or not the term was prognostic. Under correct models, the exceedance rate of its studentised maximum over a null reference for chance imbalance was 3.5–6.0% (nominal 5%) when the censoring model pooled nine intervals and mostly 1.0–4.5% under censoring in a single interval. With many early events, cumulative RRB stayed near zero, whereas the end-of-grace SMD reached 0.40; under loss to follow-up that the weights ignored, cumulative RRB departed from zero and interval RRB stayed small. In a case study, interval RRB flagged a dispensing indicator outside the censoring model. Interval RRB checks the censoring model, and cumulative RRB the representation of the baseline population.

Keywords: clone-censor-weight; target trial emulation; inverse probability of censoring weighting; covariate balance; artificial censoring; simulation study

1 Introduction

Target trial emulation specifies the protocol of a hypothetical randomised trial and emulates it with observational data 1, 2. If the initiator group of a treatment is defined at initiation and the comparison group at eligibility, the initiators are conditioned on survival to initiation, which induces immortal-time bias 3, 2. The question can then be recast as initiating within a grace period, for example 30 days from baseline, against not initiating. In the clone–censor–weight (CCW) method 4, every individual is followed under all strategies compatible with the individual’s baseline data, and artificial censoring ends each of these follow-ups at the first deviation from the allocated strategy. Inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW) corrects the resulting selection 5, 6. As the weights are estimated from a model for artificial censoring, whether they actually achieve this correction should be assessed 7, and covariate balance is widely used for this assessment.

A common diagnostic is the between-strategy standardised mean difference (SMD) of baseline covariates at the end of the grace period 7, 8, 9, 10, which a CCW primer describes as a simplified approach that excludes individuals with an event before that time 7. Jackson proposes covariate balance between censored and retained individuals (censoring balance), which is defined for loss to follow-up and for artificial censoring at protocol deviation and is applied in a CCW analysis of a randomised trial 11. The balance tables of the cobalt and WeightIt R packages compare the weighted retained individuals with the unweighted sample at risk 12, 13, and the ccwr R package summarises the weights without covariate balance 14. A systematic review of 113 CCW studies reports that 42 assessed covariate balance after weighting 15, and one applied CCW study that assesses balance states that the follow-up time at which balance should be evaluated is an unanswered question 10.

These diagnostics compare different populations, namely censored with retained individuals (censoring balance), one strategy with another (end-of-grace SMD), and the weighted retained individuals with the unweighted sample at risk (cobalt and WeightIt). They draw on a broader literature on balance between exposure groups after propensity-score matching or weighting, in which imbalance reflects confounding of the exposure. This literature includes balance diagnostics for time-varying exposures 16, 17, covariate balancing weights for time-varying treatments 18 and SMD conventions 19, 20, 21. In CCW, the imbalance of interest arises from selection by artificial censoring within each strategy, so a diagnostic must also specify the population that the weighted retained individuals should reproduce.

The comparisons also differ in their zero targets. Jackson notes that weights that produce independent censoring with respect to measured covariates should remove the imbalance between censored and retained individuals 11. Calibrated weights for loss to follow-up 22 and stable balancing weights for nonresponse 23 make the weighted retained individuals reproduce a reference sample, as the interval target below does. For the end-of-grace SMD 7, the conditions under which a correct censoring model implies a difference of zero have not been stated in the CCW setting. The balance tables of cobalt and WeightIt 12, 13 take the unweighted sample at risk as the target, which coincides with the interval target in general only in the first interval with censoring. Between strategies, the individuals at risk are the same at baseline, so the imbalance of baseline covariates after weighting arises from censoring and weighting alone, at least until outcome events deplete the strategies differently. Post-baseline covariates are affected by the treatment each strategy prescribes, so their between-strategy differences can be treatment effects. What has not been organised in CCW is the relation between each diagnostic, its reference population and its zero target, including how the weighted retained individuals, together with those who had the outcome, reconstruct the baseline population and how the diagnostics relate to between-strategy SMDs. A reference for the imbalance that chance alone produces is also lacking.

This paper makes three contributions. First, we show that, under positivity and a correct censoring model, the weighted individuals retained under a strategy reproduce the previously weighted risk set just before each censoring interval (interval target) and, together with the individuals who had the outcome, the baseline population (cumulative target). Censoring balance then has a zero target, and the end-of-grace SMD acquires a depletion term once outcome events have occurred. Second, we propose risk-set reconstruction balance (RRB), which compares the weighted retained individuals with each target population; interval RRB has a zero target for every function of the covariate history, and cumulative RRB keeps a zero target for baseline covariates after outcome events. Third, we provide a null reference for chance imbalance in the maximum of interval RRB over strata.

Section 2 introduces the setting and notation. Section 3 derives the interval and cumulative targets and defines RRB, and Section 4 constructs the null reference. Sections 5 and 6 evaluate the diagnostics in a three-part ADEMP simulation study 24, and Section 7 applies them to a public synthetic Medicare cohort. Section 8 discusses the findings, their relation to previous work and the limitations, and gives recommendations.

2 Setting and notation

We follow nn individuals over the intervals ℐk=[tk,tk+1)\mathcal{I}_{k}=[t_{k},t_{k+1}), k=0,…,K−1k=0,\dots,K-1; an outcome or artificial censoring during an interval carries its index. Individual ii has baseline covariates XiX_{i} and, for ℐk\mathcal{I}_{k}, time-varying covariates Li​kL_{ik}, treatment Ai​kA_{ik} and the binary outcome indicator Yi​kY_{ik}. If individual ii has the outcome, it occurs in ℐτi\mathcal{I}_{\tau_{i}}. The history Hi​kH_{ik} of individual ii comprises the covariates up to ℐk\mathcal{I}_{k} and the treatment before it. Within an interval, covariates, treatment, artificial censoring, loss to follow-up and the outcome occur in this order. A strategy gg is a treatment rule, for example “initiate within a window that ends with a grace period” or “do not initiate before a given interval” 6, 25. We consider strategies of treatment initiation, in which initiation is absorbing; once an individual initiates, Ai​k′=1A_{ik^{\prime}}=1 for every later interval k′k^{\prime}.

The risk-set indicator Ri​kgR^{g}_{ik} equals 1 if, at the start of ℐk\mathcal{I}_{k}, the treatment history of individual ii has remained compatible with gg, the outcome has not occurred and follow-up has not been lost. The artificial-censoring indicator Di​kgD^{g}_{ik} equals 1 if Ri​kg=1R^{g}_{ik}=1 and the treatment observed in ℐk\mathcal{I}_{k} is incompatible with gg 4, 6, 26; such an individual is absent from the risk set of the next interval. For strategy gg and interval ℐk\mathcal{I}_{k}, the individuals at risk form ℛ={i:Ri​kg=1}\mathcal{R}=\{i:R^{g}_{ik}=1\}, the censored individuals 𝒞={i∈ℛ:Di​kg=1}\mathcal{C}=\{i\in\mathcal{R}:D^{g}_{ik}=1\} and the retained individuals 𝒰=ℛ∖𝒞\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{R}\setminus\mathcal{C}. We drop ii and gg where no ambiguity arises, writing, for example, DkD_{k} for Di​kgD^{g}_{ik}, and keep gg and g′g^{\prime} only where two strategies are compared. Censoring occurs in two phases 8, 7. An individual who initiates before the window opens (under no initiation, before the given interval) is censored at initiation, and an individual who has not initiated by the last interval of the window is censored under the initiation strategy. Artificial censoring of an individual at risk is a deterministic function of AkA_{k}, so HkH_{k} excludes AkA_{k}, as conditioning on it would make the probability of censoring degenerate. In the CCW literature the record of individual ii under strategy gg is called a clone; we keep the word only in the name of the method.

Let πk=P⁡(Dk=0∣Rk=1,Hk)\pi_{k}=P(D_{k}=0\mid R_{k}=1,H_{k}) be the probability of remaining uncensored given the history, with πk=1\pi_{k}=1 where censoring cannot occur. Let qk=P⁡(Dk=0∣Rk=1)q_{k}=P(D_{k}=0\mid R_{k}=1), which is common to all individuals at risk in the strategy-by-interval stratum, hereafter stratum. The estimand is the risk P⁡(Ykg=1​ for some ​k<K)P(Y^{g}_{k}=1\text{ for some }k<K) under each strategy, where YkgY^{g}_{k} is the outcome indicator under the strategy. It is estimated by a weighted Kaplan–Meier estimator 5, 8 with the stabilised cumulative weight

Wi​k=∏l≤kqlπi​l=Qk​Wi​ku,Qk=∏l≤kql,W_{ik}=\prod_{l\leq k}\frac{q_{l}}{\pi_{il}}=Q_{k}W^{u}_{ik},\qquad Q_{k}=\prod_{l\leq k}q_{l},

where Wi​ku=∏l≤k1/πi​lW^{u}_{ik}=\prod_{l\leq k}1/\pi_{il} is the unstabilised weight 5, 27, 28, and Wi,−1=1W_{i,-1}=1. For the marginal risks estimated here, the numerator must not depend on the history; a numerator that depends on baseline covariates requires an analysis conditional on them 27, 28. A common qkq_{k} cancels within a stratum, so without truncation stabilisation affects only the scale of the weights. In the analysis, π\pi is replaced by the fitted value π^\hat{\pi} of a pooled logistic model 27, 26, and qq by the observed proportion remaining uncensored in the stratum, which keeps the same symbol. Weight concentration is summarised by stratum with the effective sample size of the retained individuals, ESS=(∑𝒰Wi​k)2/∑𝒰Wi​k2\mathrm{ESS}=(\sum_{\mathcal{U}}W_{ik})^{2}/\sum_{\mathcal{U}}W_{ik}^{2} 29, divided by the number at risk |ℛ||\mathcal{R}|, and with percentiles of their weights, such as the 99th (W99) 28, 30.

3 Reconstruction targets

Table 1 and Figure 1 summarise the diagnostics and their targets. Appendix S1 gives the derivations of (2) and (5).

The interval target is that the retained individuals, reweighted by 1/π^i1/\hat{\pi}_{i}, reproduce the risk set weighted by ww just before censoring. This local target checks the current censoring step given the earlier weights, whether or not these are correct. Define

With the residual ei=(1−Di)−π^ie_{i}=(1-D_{i})-\hat{\pi}_{i}, exactly,

∑𝒰wi​fiπ^i−∑ℛwi​fi=∑ℛwi​fi​eiπ^i,μ𝒰−μℛ=∑ℛwi​π^i−1​(fi−μℛ)​ei∑𝒰wi​π^i−1,\begin{gathered}\sum_{\mathcal{U}}\frac{w_{i}f_{i}}{\hat{\pi}_{i}}-\sum_{\mathcal{R}}w_{i}f_{i}=\sum_{\mathcal{R}}\frac{w_{i}f_{i}e_{i}}{\hat{\pi}_{i}},\\ \mu_{\mathcal{U}}-\mu_{\mathcal{R}}=\frac{\sum_{\mathcal{R}}w_{i}\hat{\pi}_{i}^{-1}(f_{i}-\mu_{\mathcal{R}})e_{i}}{\sum_{\mathcal{U}}w_{i}\hat{\pi}_{i}^{-1}},\end{gathered} (2)

so the numerator of RRB is a w/π^w/\hat{\pi}-weighted covariance between the function and the residual, each term of which has conditional mean zero under a correct model.

The score equations of the logistic model, fitted without weights, give ∑fi​ei=0\sum f_{i}e_{i}=0 over the rows of the fit for every modelled function. For a history function outside the model, ∑fi​ei\sum f_{i}e_{i} is the score for adding ff to the censoring model. If the reference weights are constant in the stratum and a model with an intercept is fitted to the stratum alone, as when artificial censoring under a strategy occurs in a single interval, the score equals ∑ℛ(fi−μℛ)​ei\sum_{\mathcal{R}}(f_{i}-\mu_{\mathcal{R}})e_{i}, and the numerator of RRB weights each term of this sum by wi/π^iw_{i}/\hat{\pi}_{i}, the weight of a retained individual in the estimator. RRB of a modelled function therefore departs from zero only through this weighting and through pooling over intervals, and diagnostic information lies mainly in history functions outside the model. For a modelled function, RRB in a single interval of a pooled fit can still reveal an association with censoring that changes across intervals. Weighting by wi/π^iw_{i}/\hat{\pi}_{i} puts RRB on the scale of the weighted risk-set mean that the estimator reconstructs. The unweighted score test, which asks whether ff improves the fit of the censoring model, remains a complementary check.

Suppose that π^\hat{\pi} is constant within the stratum. Every individual in the stratum is then censorable, so that 𝒰c=𝒰\mathcal{U}^{c}=\mathcal{U}. The means μ𝒰\mu_{\mathcal{U}} and μ𝒞\mu_{\mathcal{C}} reduce to the ww-weighted means of the retained and censored individuals, μℛ\mu_{\mathcal{R}} is their weighted average, and

RRB=−∑𝒞wi∑ℛwi​CB.\mathrm{RRB}=-\frac{\sum_{\mathcal{C}}w_{i}}{\sum_{\mathcal{R}}w_{i}}\,\mathrm{CB}.

When π^\hat{\pi} varies, RRB and CB are different statistics with the same zero target. We take interval RRB as the primary interval diagnostic. RRB requires only πk≥ε>0\pi_{k}\geq\varepsilon>0, whereas CB weights the censored individuals by (1−π^i)−1(1-\hat{\pi}_{i})^{-1}, which requires πk≤1−ε\pi_{k}\leq 1-\varepsilon for the censorable individuals and is large and variable when censoring is rare. As the two statistics have different scales, they should not share a threshold.

Truncation caps Wi​kW_{ik}, which then differs from wi/π^iw_{i}/\hat{\pi}_{i}, and interval RRB computed with the truncated weights has no zero target. It measures the imbalance that truncation leaves. The model-weight version (1), which combines the truncated reference weights ww with the untruncated inverse probabilities 1/π^1/\hat{\pi} of the current interval, keeps the zero target of Proposition 1, as does censoring balance.

Remark (depletion term). Under the conditions of Proposition 2, Δg​(k)\Delta_{g}(k) converges to −{Fg/(1−Fg)}{μ¯gY−E(f)}/SD(f)-\{F_{g}/(1-F_{g})\}\{\bar{\mu}^{Y}_{g}-E(f)\}/\mathrm{SD}(f), where FgF_{g} is the weighted cumulative incidence before ℐk\mathcal{I}_{k} under strategy gg and μ¯gY\bar{\mu}^{Y}_{g} the limit of the mean of ff among these events (Appendix S1). The limit is non-zero when events have occurred and ff is prognostic.

Under a correct censoring model, the end-of-grace SMD can therefore be non-zero once events have occurred, unless the depletion terms of the two strategies cancel. The term formalises the depletion of susceptibles, which makes even randomised groups differ in prognostic factors among survivors 31, 32, and the exclusion of individuals with an event that the primer notes 7.

Remark (loss to follow-up). Under the conditions of Proposition 2 except that individuals can be lost to follow-up, cumulative RRB converges to the limit of −λ/(1−λ)-\lambda/(1-\lambda) times the standardised difference between the lost individuals and the baseline population, where λ\lambda is the weighted share of the individuals lost while retained before ℐk\mathcal{I}_{k}, carried forward as those with an earlier event (Appendix S1).

The difference is non-zero even under completely random loss once prognostic individuals have had the outcome, as the lost individuals resemble the survivors at the times of loss. Weighting by the inverse probabilities of remaining in follow-up restores the target 33, 34.

Because between-strategy balance is a difference, it also cancels deviations common to both strategies, such as a shared misspecification of the censoring model; cumulative RRB compares each strategy with the fixed baseline population and contains neither the depletion term nor this cancellation. For a post-baseline covariate LkL_{k}, Bg​g′B_{gg^{\prime}} contains effects of the strategies on LkL_{k} even under perfect weighting 35, 36, 37 and is descriptive, without a zero target.

3.3 Unmeasured variables

Proposition 3 (unmeasured variables). Suppose that artificial censoring depends on an unmeasured UU that also affects the outcome, and that π^\hat{\pi} converges to πk​(Hk)\pi_{k}(H_{k}). Then the targets of Propositions 1 and 2 are zero, but the weighted risk is in general biased for the risk under the strategy (proof in Appendix S1).

The diagnostics thus detect misspecification in the measured history, not violations of exchangeability.

4 A null reference for the interval diagnostics

Interval RRB and censoring balance are summarised for each strategy by their maximum absolute value over the strata with artificial censoring, for example MaxIB=maxk⁡|RRB⁡(k)|\mathrm{MaxIB}=\max_{k}|\mathrm{RRB}(k)|; where stated, the maximum is also taken over history functions. In a sample, the diagnostics fluctuate around their zero targets, so these maxima are positive even under a correct censoring model.

Remark (null SD). Under a correct model, with πk\pi_{k} roughly constant in a stratum and a function unrelated to the weights, the standard deviation (SD) of RRB is approximately {(1−πk)/ESS}1/2\{(1-\pi_{k})/\mathrm{ESS}\}^{1/2} (Appendix S1).

The null SD thus grows with the share censored and with weight concentration, and the maximum of mm approximately independent standard normal values is about 2​log⁡m\sqrt{2\log m}. A threshold such as 0.1 therefore has no fixed false-positive rate. The sampling variability of SMDs has been studied for two-group comparisons at a single time point, with a Bonferroni-corrected critical value for the maximum studentised excess of the SMDs over 0.1 38, and a randomisation-based omnibus test covers stratified and clustered designs 39. In person-interval data by strategy, censoring is sequential and the records of one individual enter several intervals and strata, which makes a resampling reference natural.

The package function rrb_null() provides a parametric reference distribution for chance imbalance under a correct censoring model, hereafter the null reference. In each stratum, conditional on the observed risk set and reference weights ww, it redraws the censoring indicators, Dk∗∼Bernoulli⁡(1−π^)D^{*}_{k}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(1-\hat{\pi}), on every row where censoring is possible, refits the censoring model and recomputes interval RRB, in its model-weight version (1) under weight truncation, and censoring balance, ndrawsn_{\mathrm{draws}} times. For both statistics, it reports each stratum’s null SD and zz, the ratio of the observed value to it, and, for each strategy, the studentised maximum, the largest |z||z| over its strata and the history functions (excluding strata with a null SD of 0), with the 95th percentile of the same maximum over the draws and the exceedance probability; the same quantities are reported for MaxIB. The records of one individual under different strategies are coupled through one uniform variate per individual and interval, which keeps every row’s marginal 1−π^1-\hat{\pi} and is approximate when the strategy-specific models disagree (Appendix S2). Redrawn censoring is not propagated to later risk sets or to Wk−1W_{k-1}, as propagation would require models for the covariates and outcomes of individuals after their censoring, so the reference applies to the interval target only.

Each strategy is judged against the reference of its own censoring model by its studentised maximum. The null SD of RRB differs between strata, through the share censored and the ESS (Remark above), and between history functions, so MaxIB is dominated by the strata with much censoring, whereas division by the null SD puts every stratum and history function on the same footing. MaxIB is reported as a descriptive summary on the scale of the diagnostic (Appendix S2).

In an oracle setting (fixed risk sets and weights, known censoring probabilities, no refit), the redraw gives the exact conditional null distribution of each stratum’s RRB. The implementation replaces the known probabilities by fitted ones, refits the model and holds the realised dependence between strata fixed, so its calibration is examined empirically, with an oracle check and a per-strategy decomposition (Table S1; Section 6.2). The null reference is therefore a diagnostic reference distribution with approximate calibration, and its exceedance probability indicates how unusual the observed imbalance is under the fitted model; it is not the size of a formal test. An exceedance is evidence of misspecification of the censoring model with respect to the measured history, subject to this calibration and to the multiplicity of the strata and history functions examined. A non-exceedance is weak evidence of a correct model, and its reassurance depends on the same calibration, on the ESS and on the distribution of the history function.

5 Simulation study

We follow the ADEMP structure 24.

5.1 Aims

The simulation study has three parts. Part 1 shows that the interval diagnostics of Section 3.1 respond to an omitted term’s effect on censoring, whether or not the term is prognostic, whereas bias requires outcome-related selection. Part 2 examines the calibration of the null reference of Section 4, with many history functions and under unstable weights. Part 3 examines the cumulative and between-strategy targets of Section 3.2 under treatment→\tocovariate effects, under depletion and under loss to follow-up that the weights ignore, and the variability of cumulative RRB.

5.2 Data-generating mechanisms

A baseline covariate X∼N⁡(0,1)X\sim N(0,1) and a time-varying covariate LkL_{k}, autoregressive and affected by prior treatment with coefficient α2\alpha_{2}, determine absorbing treatment initiation (logistic in LkL_{k}, Lk2L_{k}^{2}, XX, Lk​XL_{k}X and Lk−1L_{k-1}, coefficients β\beta), optional covariate-dependent loss to follow-up, and a binary outcome over 12 intervals (logistic, coefficients γ\gamma; Appendix S2), in the order of Section 2. The initiation hazard does not depend on the interval, so the censoring models contain no time terms. The strategies are initiation in intervals 0–2 (g1g_{1}), initiation in intervals 0–8 (g2g_{2}), and no initiation through interval 8 (g3g_{3}). Under the initiation strategies, an individual who has not initiated by the last interval of the window deviates in that interval; under g3g_{3}, an individual deviates at initiation in intervals 0–8, and initiation from interval 9 onwards is allowed. The contrast of g2g_{2} against g1g_{1} concerns the length of the initiation window, and that of g3g_{3} against g2g_{2} initiation within the window against no initiation.

The three parts (Table 2) have n=2,000n=2{,}000 unless stated. Part 1 (censoring-model misspecification and estimation bias) omits LkL_{k}, Lk2L_{k}^{2} or Lk−1L_{k-1} from the artificial-censoring model, one term at a time, and crosses the censoring strength, the coefficient of the omitted term in the treatment model, which determines censoring (weak or strong), with the outcome strength, its coefficient in the outcome model (none or strong). For omitted LkL_{k}, the treatment model also lacks Lk2L_{k}^{2} and Lk​XL_{k}X, and for omitted Lk2L_{k}^{2} it lacks Lk​XL_{k}X, so each omitted term defines its own mechanism. With the correct model, Part 1 has 13 scenarios.

Part 2 (null-reference calibration and weight instability) has scenarios with correct specification at n=300n=300, 2,000 (shared with Part 1) and 8,000 (1,000, 1,000 and 500 replicates; 200 in every other scenario), near-violation of positivity, weight truncation and extreme weights, and one scenario at n=300n=300 that adds eight baseline covariates X2,…,X9X_{2},\dots,X_{9} with correlation ρ=0.5\rho=0.5 with XX, all modelled and monitored (16 history functions; about 175 combinations of stratum and history function, against 87 in the base mechanism).

Part 3 (reconstruction targets) covers scenarios without and with a strong treatment→\tocovariate effect, covariate-dependent loss to follow-up that the weights ignore, and many early events under a correct model, which make the depletion term large. Coefficients were chosen so that the predicted phenomena are visible.

5.3 Estimands

The true risk under a grace-period strategy (g1g_{1}, g2g_{2}) is that of the natural grace-period regime, in which initiation occurs at its natural time and is forced in the last interval of the grace period for individuals who have not initiated 25; CCW targets this regime for a strategy of initiation within a window 40. The true risk under g3g_{3} is that of the regime in which no individual initiates in intervals 0–8 and initiation follows its natural course from interval 9 onwards. The estimands are the risk differences at the end of follow-up without loss to follow-up, θ21\theta_{21} (g2g_{2} minus g1g_{1}) and θ32\theta_{32} (g3g_{3} minus g2g_{2}), whose true values were computed from 5×1055\times 10^{5} individuals simulated under each regime (Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE) about 7×10−47\times 10^{-4}).

5.4 Methods

Pooled logistic artificial-censoring models were fitted by strategy over its censoring intervals. The correct model contained LkL_{k}, Lk2L_{k}^{2}, XX and Lk​XL_{k}X (and X2,…,X9X_{2},\dots,X_{9} in the scenario with many covariates). Risks were estimated by a weighted discrete-time Kaplan–Meier estimator, with normal-approximation 95% confidence intervals (CIs) from a bootstrap standard error (SE) 41, 8 that resampled individuals, with their records under all strategies, and refitted the censoring model. The diagnostics, summarised as in Section 4 over the intervals with artificial censoring of each strategy, were interval RRB and censoring balance (censorable individuals) for XX, LkL_{k}, Lk2L_{k}^{2}, Lk​Lk−1L_{k}L_{k-1}, Lk−Lk−1L_{k}-L_{k-1}, the cumulative mean of LL, I⁡(Lk>0)I(L_{k}>0) and Lk​XL_{k}X (and X2,…,X9X_{2},\dots,X_{9}); cumulative RRB of XX and L0L_{0}, summarised by its maximum absolute value over the same intervals, the strategies and the two functions; and the end-of-grace SMD of XX at interval 3 for g2g_{2} against g1g_{1} and at interval 9 for g3g_{3} against g2g_{2}, the first intervals after the grace periods of g1g_{1} and g2g_{2}. In every replicate, the null reference (500 draws) determined, for each strategy, whether the studentised maximum of interval RRB over all history functions, that of each history function, that of censoring balance and MaxIB exceeded its null 95th percentile. Under weight truncation, interval RRB was computed with the truncated weights of the estimator, and the null reference computed interval RRB and censoring balance with untruncated inverse probabilities 1/π^1/\hat{\pi}, as in the model-weight version (1). The bootstrap also gave a percentile 95% interval for cumulative RRB of XX under each strategy at intervals 3 and 9. The bootstrap had 100 resamples, and 500 in the scenarios with correct specification at n=300n=300 and 2,000, near-violation of positivity, weight truncation and many early events (200 at n=8,000n=8{,}000). We recorded the smallest ESS/|ℛ||\mathcal{R}| and the largest W99 over all intervals and strategies, and the maximum between-strategy SMD of LL.

5.5 Performance measures

The performance measures for θ^21\hat{\theta}_{21} and θ^32\hat{\theta}_{32} were the bias, the Monte Carlo standard deviation of the estimates (MCSD), the absolute bias over the MCSD, the coverage and the ratio of the mean bootstrap SE to the MCSD. Each diagnostic was summarised by its mean. Biases, coverages and means are reported with their MCSEs. For the factorial design of Part 1, the main effects and interaction of censoring strength and outcome strength were computed for the bias and for interval RRB. The exceedance rate is the proportion of replicates in which a maximum exceeded its null 95th percentile or, for cumulative RRB, the bootstrap interval excluded 0. It is a false-positive rate (nominal 0.05) under a correct model and a detection rate otherwise. Replicates in which the studentised maximum was undefined, because every null draw reproduced the observed RRB in every stratum, were excluded. As each omitted term defines its own mechanism, mean diagnostics are compared only among the scenarios with the same omitted term.

6 Simulation results

6.1 Part 1: censoring-model misspecification and estimation bias

Substantial bias arose only when the omitted term affected both censoring and outcome, directly or through correlated prognostic terms, and it was concentrated in θ^32\hat{\theta}_{32} (Figure 2, Table 3). The interaction contrast of its bias was −0.048-0.048 to −0.025-0.025 (MCSE 0.003; Table S5). With strong censoring and outcome strengths, its bias was 1.7 to 3.9 MCSDs and its coverage 0.020 to 0.485. With an outcome strength of none, its absolute bias was at most 1.00 MCSD (omitted Lk−1L_{k-1} with strong censoring strength; coverage 0.730). Under g3g_{3}, a misspecified model acts on the weights in each of the nine censoring intervals, which is consistent with the larger bias of θ^32\hat{\theta}_{32}.

The interval diagnostics followed mainly the censoring strength. Over the three omitted terms, the main effect of censoring strength on MaxIB was 0.15 to 0.26 under g1g_{1}, 0.01 to 0.10 under g2g_{2} and 0.01 to 0.06 under g3g_{3}, and the main effects of outcome strength were small (−0.013-0.013 to 0.016; Table S5). Detection depended on the strategy and rose with censoring strength (Table 3). It was highest under g3g_{3} (0.770 to 1.000), whose model is fitted over nine intervals, and lowest under g2g_{2} (0.185 to 0.985), whose single censoring interval has fewer censorable individuals than that of g1g_{1} (Table S1). Omitted Lk−1L_{k-1} was detected mainly through Lk−Lk−1L_{k}-L_{k-1}, whose own studentised maximum exceeded its reference in 0.400 to 1.000 of replicates (Table S2), whereas under g3g_{3} MaxIB exceeded its own reference in only 0.075 to 0.130 (Table S2). Censoring balance, with its own null reference, detected the same mechanisms. Neither statistic was uniformly more sensitive (Table S4).

6.2 Part 2: null-reference calibration and weight instability

Under correct censoring models, the exceedance rate of the studentised maximum was 0.035 to 0.060 under g3g_{3} and 0.010 to 0.045 under g1g_{1} and g2g_{2}, and that of censoring balance 0.006 to 0.065 (Figure 3, Table 4 and Table S2); the exception was g2g_{2} with 16 history functions (below). For single history functions, the exceedance rate was 0.000 to 0.085 (Table S2). MaxIB averaged 0.156 to 0.195 at n=300n=300 and 0.362 for g3g_{3} under near-violation of positivity, above the conventional 0.1 (Table S3).

In the oracle setting of Section 4 (scheme S5 of Table S1), exceedance of the studentised maximum was 0.038 to 0.061 for the three strategies. The per-strategy decomposition of Table S1 located the shortfall of g1g_{1} and g2g_{2} in the redraw from the fitted probabilities. At n=2,000n=2{,}000, the redraw from the true probabilities with refitting gave 0.050 to 0.065, and the redraw from π^\hat{\pi} without refitting gave 0.002 to 0.038, so refitting is necessary. Under g1g_{1} and g2g_{2}, the shortfall was largest for the modelled terms (0.011 to 0.027, against 0.025 to 0.050 for the other functions; Table S2), consistent with the score equations nearly balancing them (Section 3.1).

With 16 history functions at n=300n=300, the exceedance rate under g2g_{2} was 0.107 (SE 0.023), above the nominal 0.05, and at most 0.040 under the other strategies and for censoring balance (Table 4); the single history functions of g2g_{2} exceeded their references in 0.043 to 0.171 of replicates.

Under correct specification at n=2,000n=2{,}000 and 8,000, coverage was 0.937 to 0.954. At n=300n=300, it was 0.896 for θ^21\hat{\theta}_{21} and 0.923 for θ^32\hat{\theta}_{32} (MCSE 0.010 and 0.008), below the nominal 0.95. The SE ratio was 0.91 to 1.01 for θ^21\hat{\theta}_{21} and 0.70 to 0.85 for θ^32\hat{\theta}_{32}. A few outlying replicates inflated the MCSD of θ^32\hat{\theta}_{32}; with the interquartile range, its SE ratio was 1.03 to 1.11 (Appendix S2). Truncation gave the most favourable weights (smallest ESS/|ℛ||\mathcal{R}| 0.191, largest W99 1.55; base scenario 0.113 and 9.38) but an absolute bias of 0.93 MCSD for θ^21\hat{\theta}_{21} (coverage 0.895) and of 1.64 MCSD for θ^32\hat{\theta}_{32} (coverage 0.615). With the weights of the estimator, MaxIB of interval RRB was 0.274 and 0.201 under g1g_{1} and g2g_{2} (base scenario 0.064 and 0.050), cumulative RRB 0.266 (0.095), and the two end-of-grace SMDs were 0.28 and 0.44 (0.02 and 0.09; Table S3). With the model weights of the null reference, MaxIB was close to that of the base scenario under g1g_{1} and g2g_{2} and smaller under g3g_{3} (Table S3). Under extreme weights (coverage of θ^32\hat{\theta}_{32} 0.500; SE ratio 0.62) and near-violation of positivity (0.650; 0.60), the exceedance rate was 0.015 to 0.060, so the null reference does not flag extreme weights.

6.3 Part 3: reconstruction targets

Without a treatment→\tocovariate effect, the maximum between-strategy SMD of LL for g3g_{3} against g2g_{2} was 0.11; it was 0.90 with the default effect and 2.64 with the strong effect (0.11 to 1.27 for the other contrast). MaxIB of interval RRB, the bias of both contrasts (at most 0.10 MCSD) and the exceedance rate (0.010 to 0.055) did not change systematically (Tables S2 and S3). With LkL_{k} omitted (Part 1), the same SMD was 0.82 to 0.88, so between-strategy balance of LL would have flagged the valid analysis with a strong effect and missed the biased ones.

By the end of the grace period of g1g_{1}, 5.4% of individuals had the outcome in the base scenario and 35.8% with many early events, under which the depletion term became visible. The end-of-grace SMD of XX was 0.056 at interval 3 and 0.403 at interval 9, against 0.015 and 0.089 in the base scenario, whereas cumulative RRB was 0.049 (base scenario 0.095). The exceedance rate was 0.010 to 0.050 (Table S2), the bias was 0.23 MCSD for θ^21\hat{\theta}_{21} and 0.05 MCSD for θ^32\hat{\theta}_{32}, and coverage was 0.925 and 0.945 (Table S3).

When the weights ignored covariate-dependent loss to follow-up, the bias of θ^32\hat{\theta}_{32} was 2.5 MCSDs (coverage 0.290) and that of θ^21\hat{\theta}_{21} 0.9 MCSD (coverage 0.890). MaxIB of interval RRB (at most 0.090; exceedance rate 0.015 to 0.035; Tables S2 and S3) and the end-of-grace SMD at interval 3 (0.028) stayed small because the artificial-censoring model was correct. The end-of-grace SMD at interval 9 was 0.234, smaller than under many early events with a correct model, so this SMD does not separate loss to follow-up from depletion. Cumulative RRB was 0.448 (Table S3).

Under correct models the bootstrap interval of cumulative RRB of XX excluded 0 in 0.017 to 0.095 of replicates at interval 3, after the end of the grace period of g1g_{1}, and in 0.016 to 0.211 at interval 9, after the end of the grace period of g2g_{2}, highest under g3g_{3} after prolonged censoring with concentrated weights (Table S6). The individual bootstrap interval is thus anti-conservative for the cumulative target.

7 Case study

7.1 Setting

We re-analysed the public cohort of the Webster-Clark CCW tutorial 40, which was built from the 2008–2010 Data Entrepreneurs’ Synthetic Public Use File (DE-SynPUF) of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. The cohort comprises 1,590 patients discharged after myocardial infarction, followed for initiation of antiplatelet treatment and for rehospitalisation or death within 180 days. We linked the cohort file, which records baseline covariates only, to the DE-SynPUF claims and derived, for each individual and interval, three indicators of healthcare use in the 10 days before the interval began, namely a physician claim, a hospital outpatient claim and a dispensing of a drug other than the index antiplatelet (present in 54%, 13% and 58% of individual-intervals). From the dispensing history we also derived three depth functions, namely the indicator of the preceding window (10 to 19 days before the interval; present in 54%), the number of dispensings in the 30 days before the interval (mean 3.1) and the number since discharge (mean 8.9).

Three strategies (initiation within days 0–29 or 0–89, and no initiation before day 90, after which initiation was allowed) were analysed in 10-day intervals. We took the tutorial’s artificial-censoring model, with age, sex, end-stage renal disease and, in the phase in which initiating causes censoring, interval-number terms, as the pre-specified model. The eleven monitored history functions were the five baseline covariates (age, sex, renal disease and two race indicators), the three use indicators and the three depth functions, which remained outside every model and test whether the 10-day indicator summarises the dispensing history. No function was designated as primary in advance, so the function-specific comparisons are exploratory (Section 8.4). Cumulative RRB was computed for the five baseline covariates, with 95% percentile intervals of the individual bootstrap (200 resamples), and the null reference had 500 draws. The associations of the use indicators with initiation and with the outcome were estimated by pooled logistic regression in the individual-intervals at risk under no initiation before day 90, given age, sex, renal disease and interval. Following the usual convention, and unlike Section 2, censoring for non-initiation was realised at the end of the last interval of a window, after its outcomes and losses to follow-up, whose individuals stayed in the risk set with π^=1\hat{\pi}=1; this keeps the zero targets of interval and cumulative RRB and removes that of censoring balance (Appendix S1). The case study therefore does not report censoring balance. Loss to follow-up was rare (30 of the 1,590 patients before day 180, 8 by day 90) and was not weighted. By the identity of Section 3.2, a lost share of 0.005 and survivor-versus-baseline differences of at most 0.17 bound its contribution to cumulative RRB at about 0.001, if the lost patients resemble the survivors and the weights do not concentrate on them.

7.2 Results

The 180-day risks were 0.414 and 0.378 for initiation within days 0–29 and 0–89 (risk difference −0.036-0.036 [−0.132-0.132, 0.0600.060]), close to those from the tutorial’s code (0.404 and 0.357; Table 5). Under the two initiation strategies, 83% of the risk set was censored in days 20–29 (hereafter day 30) and 60% in days 80–89 (hereafter day 90); under no initiation before day 90, 4% to 7% was censored in each interval. Weighting reduced ||RRB|| of the modelled covariates below 0.03 at day 30 and day 90 (Table S7). Cumulative RRB of the five baseline covariates stayed within ±0.015\pm 0.015 over the nine censoring intervals, and at day 90 every 95% bootstrap interval included zero (Figure 4C).

By day 90, 25.0% of the cohort had the outcome. For end-stage renal disease, the most prognostic baseline covariate, the depletion term in the interval beginning on day 90 was −0.086-0.086 to −0.071-0.071 under the three strategies, in agreement with the approximation of Section 3.2 (−0.082-0.082), whereas cumulative RRB was −0.012-0.012 to 0.002. The end-of-grace SMD was −0.006-0.006 between the two initiation strategies, whose depletion terms cancelled, and −0.024-0.024 and −0.030-0.030 against no initiation.

A dispensing in the preceding 10 days predicted initiation in the interval (odds ratio 1.37) and not the outcome (1.12), whereas the physician and outpatient indicators predicted the outcome (1.44 and 1.40) and not initiation. Outside the censoring model, the dispensing indicator kept an interval RRB of 0.245 at day 30 and 0.190 at day 90 after weighting (Figure 4A). Its studentised maximum exceeded the null 95th percentile under both initiation strategies (p=0.020p=0.020 and 0.024; Figure 4B) and fell just short of it under no initiation before day 90 (p=0.056p=0.056). The three depth functions had RRB of 0.159 to 0.195 at day 90, and the 30-day count exceeded its reference under two strategies (p=0.024p=0.024 and 0.026). The maximum over all eleven functions stayed within its reference under every strategy (Table 5). Race other than white or Black (prevalence 6%, outside the model) had an interval RRB of −0.112-0.112 at day 90 under initiation within days 0–89 and stayed within its reference (p=0.218p=0.218), but an ESS/|ℛ||\mathcal{R}| of 0.105 limits what this non-exceedance shows.

Adding the three use indicators to both phases of the censoring model reduced the interval RRB of the dispensing indicator to 0.018 at day 30 and 0.000 at day 90. The studentised maxima of the dispensing indicator, of the depth functions (RRB 0.077 to 0.132 at day 90; p≥0.116p\geq 0.116) and over all eleven functions then stayed within their references (Figure 4B and Table 5); race other stayed at −0.110-0.110. At day 90 under initiation within days 0–89, ESS/|ℛ||\mathcal{R}| fell from 0.105 to 0.095, the 99th weight percentile rose from 6.6 to 8.7, and the risk difference moved from −0.036-0.036 to −0.045-0.045 (Table 5).

The evidence of misspecification rests on 4 of the 33 single-function comparisons within a strategy (pp from 0.020 to 0.026; two more had p=0.050p=0.050), all concerning the dispensing history; with no function designated in advance, these exploratory findings identify a candidate revision. As the score equations nearly balance modelled functions (Section 3.1), the evidence that the revision improved the reconstruction rests on the depth functions, which stayed outside both models, and cumulative RRB was unchanged. The revised model was selected with diagnostics from the same data, and its confidence interval does not reflect this selection. We report it as the primary analysis of this illustration and the tutorial’s model as a sensitivity analysis; under either, ESS/|ℛ||\mathcal{R}| of about 0.1 at day 90 leaves the estimate for initiation within days 0–89 dependent on few retained individuals.

8 Discussion

8.1 Principal findings

Risk-set reconstruction balance measures how far the weighted retained individuals depart from the risk set just before censoring (interval RRB) and from the baseline population (cumulative RRB), the two populations that correct weights reconstruct (Propositions 1 and 2). In the simulation, interval RRB responded to an omitted term’s effect on censoring whether or not the term was prognostic. Under correct models, the exceedance rate of its studentised maximum was near the nominal level when the censoring model pooled nine intervals and below it under censoring in a single interval. Unstable weights lowered the coverage of θ^32\hat{\theta}_{32} to between 0.500 and 0.650 without raising the exceedance rate, so weight instability is assessed with the ESS and the weight percentiles. With many early events, cumulative RRB stayed near zero under correct weights, whereas the end-of-grace SMD departed from zero through the depletion term; under loss to follow-up that the weights ignored, cumulative RRB departed from zero and interval RRB stayed small. In the case study, exploratory comparisons flagged the dispensing indicator, and after the revision the functions outside the model stayed within their references, cumulative RRB was unchanged and the weights became more concentrated.

8.2 Relation to previous work

The propositions follow from standard properties of inverse probability weighting. The contribution lies in assigning each diagnostic in use its reference population and the conditions under which it has a zero target. Jackson defines censored-versus-retained balance measures for loss to follow-up and for artificial censoring at protocol deviation 11. By Proposition 1 the measure for artificial censoring has the same zero target as interval RRB. The balance tables of cobalt and WeightIt 12, 13 compare the retained individuals, weighted by the product of the weights of all listed models, with the unweighted risk set, standardised by its unweighted standard deviation. This comparison coincides with interval RRB if two conditions hold. The earlier weights Wk−1W_{k-1} are constant in the risk set, as in the first interval with censoring, and the weights of the retained individuals include no censoring model of a later interval. Otherwise, the reference lacks the earlier weights or the weights of the retained individuals include later intervals, and the comparison has in general no zero target under a correct censoring model. Calibrated censoring weights 22 impose balancing conditions of the same form during estimation, and covariate balancing propensity scores 42 impose analogous conditions on treatment weights. If conditions of this form hold exactly in the same stratum and against the same reference as RRB, the RRB of the functions they contain is zero by construction, and the diagnostic information lies in the functions outside the conditions. The CCW weights standardise the retained individuals to the baseline covariate distribution 26, as per-protocol weights make adherence independent of the measured prognostic factors 43; a comparison with the baseline population restricted to survivors carries the depletion term of (5).

The null reference proposed here judges RRB against its chance variation under the fitted censoring model and therefore resembles a balance test 39, 38. Imai, King and Stuart argue that balance tests are inappropriate stopping rules for matching, because balance is a property of the sample and test results depend on the sample size 44. The null reference tests the specification of the censoring model, not the balance of the sample, as the test of over-identifying restrictions for covariate balancing propensity scores tests the specification of the propensity score model 42. The power of the null reference still depends on the sample size, so RRB is reported as a descriptive quantity, together with the null reference and the ESS.

8.3 Limitations and future work

Imbalance and bias need not agree. The diagnostics can flag imbalance in a function that is not prognostic, and a small RRB does not establish that the effect estimate is unbiased, for example when an omitted covariate is strongly correlated with modelled functions. Detection depends on which history functions are monitored, and no set of functions guarantees it. In strata with few censored individuals or a small ESS, a few weights dominate the diagnostics. The calibration of the null reference is approximate. Its exceedance rate was below the nominal level for strategies with a single censoring interval and could exceed it when few censoring events support many model parameters; a calibrated variant remains future work. Cumulative RRB has no null reference, as one would require models for the covariate and outcome histories after censoring. The simulation had at most nine baseline covariates, one time-varying covariate, absorbing initiation and 12 intervals, and the case study involved an omission known in advance. More time-varying covariates, more severe violations of positivity and sustained strategies remain to be studied.

8.4 Recommendations

We recommend reporting three checks, each for a different failure mechanism. (i) Misspecification of the artificial-censoring model is checked by interval RRB or censoring balance, with the studentised maximum of each strategy against the null reference. (ii) Loss of representation of the baseline population, through loss to follow-up that the weights ignore or weight truncation, is checked by cumulative RRB of baseline covariates up to the end of the grace period, reported as a descriptive trajectory. (iii) Weight concentration is checked by the ESS and weight percentiles by stratum. The end-of-grace SMD has no zero target once events have occurred, and between-strategy SMDs of post-baseline covariates have none.

As the score equations nearly balance the functions in the model, the monitored set should include history functions outside it. A few of these should be specified in advance and compared with their own null references, and further comparisons are exploratory. An exceedance prompts a revision of the specification, which is judged by the three checks together, and the effect estimate is reported under both models.

8.5 Conclusion

In CCW analyses under positivity and a correct censoring model, the weighted individuals retained under a strategy reconstruct the risk set before each censoring interval and the baseline population. Risk-set reconstruction balance measures how far the weighted retained individuals depart from these two populations. Interval RRB has a zero target for every history function and, judged against the null reference for chance imbalance, can serve as a check of the censoring model. Cumulative RRB keeps a zero target for baseline covariates after outcome events and can serve as a check of the representation of the baseline population.

Data availability statement

The R package ccwbalance (version 0.1.0), the code and the definitions of the simulation scenarios that reproduce every table and figure, and the saved simulation outputs they read are available in the GitHub repository https://github.com/Nonokyu/ccwbalance and archived at Zenodo (doi: 10.5281/zenodo.24013295). The Webster-Clark SynPUF cohort is public and available with the tutorial code at https://github.com/mawcpharmdphd/CCW_tutorial, and the DE-SynPUF claims are public at the website of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. The repository of this work contains the scripts that extract the cohort’s claims, derive the time-varying indicators and re-create the empirical outputs.

Software

The diagnostics are implemented in the R package ccwbalance, version 0.1.0 (this work), developed and run in R 4.4.3, and the repository reproduces every table and figure. The package also handles sustained strategies, in which artificial censoring can occur in every interval. Appendix S4 describes its handling of edge cases and weight truncation.

Supporting Information

Appendix S1: propositions and proofs. Appendix S2: simulation study, with the data-generating mechanisms of Parts 1–3, the coupling of the null reference within individuals, a per-strategy decomposition of its exceedance shortfall (Table S1), the dependence of MaxIB on the scale of the history functions, robust SE ratios under correct specification, null-reference exceedance by history function (Table S2), performance and diagnostics of Parts 1–3 (Table S3), detection by interval RRB and censoring balance at nominal and at matched empirical size (Table S4), factorial contrasts of Part 1 (Table S5) and bootstrap intervals of cumulative RRB (Table S6). Appendix S3: case study, with interval RRB at the grace-period ends (Table S7). Appendix S4: implementation details of the package.
